transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I suppose what brings me in is... well, it's a bit hard to explain, but I just can't get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. I mean, I know I'm 62 and I've spent my whole life working the land, doing agricultural work, out in the sun and the wind and the dirt, and you expect some wear and tear, right? But it's more than that. It's like... every time I have to go into town, say, to talk to the banker about a loan for the season, or if I have to go to the county office for some paperwork, I just feel this heavy weight, this absolute certainty that they aren't listening to a word I say. I feel like they're just staring at me. Staring at the deep cracks in my hands, the dark sun spots all over my cheeks, the way the skin is just sagging around my jawline now. It’s all I can think about. I sit there in those nice, clean, air-conditioned offices across from these folks in their crisp shirts, and I just feel like this... this grotesque, weathered thing. My wife, bless her heart, she tries to talk me down. She tells me, "You just look like a man who's worked outdoors his whole life, it's nothing to be ashamed of." And I hear her, I really do, but it doesn't change what I see in the mirror or how I feel when I'm around other people. It’s just consuming me, honestly, this constant worry about how damaged I look to everyone else.
Is it only your appearance that's been bothering you, or are there other things about yourself that you worry about what others think of?

Well, let me think on that... no, honestly, it really is just the physical side of things. Just the way I look. Because, see, I know my business. I went to college for a couple of years back in the day before I took over the land full-time, so I understand the economics of it all. When I go in to talk to the loan officer, I have my spreadsheets, my yield projections, my soil data... I know I'm competent. I don't sit there worrying that they think I'm a fool or that I don't know how to manage my crops. I've been doing this for forty years, you know? I'm a good neighbor, I treat my wife well... I don't have any doubts about my character or my mind, I suppose you could say. 

It's just... it's just this shell I'm walking around in. The face, the hands. It just overrides everything else. I can be sitting there making a perfectly sound argument about fertilizer costs or equipment depreciation, but in my head, I'm just thinking, "He's not hearing a word of this, he's just staring at that massive, dark sunspot on my left temple, he's looking at how my knuckles are just cracked and brown like old saddle leather." It's like the appearance just completely eclipses all the good things I know about myself. So, no, I don't worry about my personality or my intelligence or anything like that... it always just comes right back to this... this ruined, worn-out skin.
Has your worry about how you look affected your daily activities or relationships with others?

Well... yes, I suppose it has. It really has, and that’s the hardest part to admit, honestly. You see, it’s not just a passing thought anymore, it’s started to really interfere with how I run things. Just last month, for instance, we were supposed to be finalizing the operating loan for the spring planting. I had the appointment set with the bank, a Zoom call actually, since they’re doing a lot of that now. I spent... gosh, I must have spent an hour in the bathroom before that call, just staring at the monitor, trying to adjust the lighting, trying to position the camera so the shadows wouldn't highlight the deep creases around my mouth or that big sunspot I told you about. I tried putting some of my wife's lotion on my hands to soften them up, but they just looked greasy and cracked instead of just dry and cracked. 

I got so worked up, my chest was tight, and I just couldn't do it. I couldn't bear the thought of that banker sitting in his pristine home office, looking at my face blown up on his screen. So, I canceled. I told them we had an equipment emergency. I've put off several important farm decisions like that recently because I just can't get myself looking... acceptable enough to sit down with people, even over a computer screen. 

And it’s affecting the side business, too. My wife and I, we run a little agritourism thing on the side—a small retreat on the property, and we sell some homemade crafts and preserves, that sort of thing. It helps smooth out the income when crop prices dip. My wife wanted to update the website, get some new photos of us working the land, you know, to show the "authentic farm experience" or whatever the marketing folks call it. The photographer came out, had all these ideas about catching us at golden hour, the sun setting behind the tractor. But I just flat out refused. I told her I wouldn't do it. I can't have pictures of this... this face, these hands, plastered all over the internet for anyone to zoom in on and scrutinize. She was so disappointed, and I felt terrible about it, I really did. But I just couldn't agree to those photos. It’s like I’m hiding away on my own land, and I know it’s not right, but I just can't push past it.
Are you avoiding social interactions or important activities because of your concerns about how you look?

Well, yes, I suppose I just gave you a couple of big examples of that, didn't I? The loan meeting and the photos for the retreat website. But... it's not just the big things. It's the little things, too. It's everyday stuff that I used to just do without a second thought. 

Like, going into town to pick up parts at the supply store. I used to just hop in the truck, drive into town, chat with the guys behind the counter, maybe grab a coffee at the diner next door and catch up on the local news with whoever was sitting at the counter. Now... well, now I try to time it so I'm going in right when they open, or right before they close, when I know there won't be a crowd. And if I pull up and see three or four trucks parked out front, guys I've known for decades, mind you... sometimes I just keep driving. I'll drive right past, maybe go to the next town over, which is an extra thirty minutes out of my way, or I'll just go home and try again the next day. 

Because I just can't stand the thought of standing in that bright fluorescent lighting in the store, handing over my credit card, and having them look at my hands. Or having them look at my face while we're talking about the weather. I just feel like they're cataloging every wrinkle, every spot, every rough patch. 

And church... church has been really hard. My wife and I, we've sat in the same pew for thirty years. But lately, I've been finding excuses to stay home. I'll say my back is acting up, or I need to check on the irrigation system, or I'm just too tired from the week. Because sitting there in the pews, with people turning around to shake hands during the peace, or talking out in the foyer afterward... it's just too much exposure. I feel like everyone is looking at me and thinking, "My goodness, look how awful he looks, look how the sun has just ruined him." 

So, yes, I am avoiding things. I'm avoiding a lot of things. And it's making my world very, very small. It's just me, my wife, and the fields now, mostly. And even then, I'm constantly aware of it. It's exhausting, doctor, it really is. It's like a full-time job just trying to figure out how to get through the day without having to let anyone see me.
Is it the specific features like the sunspots, wrinkles, and cracked hands that bother you, or is it more a general feeling of not looking good enough?

Well, it’s... no, it’s definitely the specific things. Very specific. It’s exactly what you just said. It’s not just some vague, general feeling of, oh, I’m getting older or I’m not a handsome man anymore. It’s... what brings me in here, what really drove me to finally talk to someone, is that I just cannot get past how incredibly rough and worn my face and my hands look. 

I mean, I can look in the mirror and I know every single mark. It’s the deep, ingrained cracks on my knuckles, it’s those dark sunspots that look like dirt that won't wash off, and it's the way the skin is just sagging and hanging around my jaw and my neck now. It's those exact features. Because when I have to go into town, or if I'm sitting across the desk from a banker or one of the county extension agents, I just know—I feel it in my gut—that they aren't listening to my business plan or my yield numbers. They are just staring right at the cracks. They're staring at the spots and the sagging skin. I feel like it's the only thing they can see, like it's magnified under a bright light. 

My wife, bless her heart, she tries to talk me down about it. She’ll look at me and say I’m being ridiculous. She tells me that I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors his whole life. She says, 'You’ve been out in the sun and the wind and the dirt for forty years, of course your hands are going to be rough, you look like a farmer.' And I suppose logically, I hear the words she's saying. I know I've worked hard. I know the elements take a toll. But I just can't see it the way she does. She sees a man who works outdoors, but I see this... this ruined, damaged skin that everyone else is judging me for. I can't just brush it off as character or a hard day's work. So, yes, it’s very specific. The spots, the cracks, the sagging... it's all of those exact things, and it just takes over my whole mind.
Do you feel like your concerns about how you look are affecting your relationships with your family, beyond just your wife?

Well, yes, it does, because... well, it all ties together, you see. We have two grown kids, and a couple of grandkids, and while they don't live right here in the main house anymore, this farm is really our family's legacy. It's a family operation. So when I'm failing to do my part, it ripples out and affects everyone. 

Like I was telling you earlier about that operating loan... missing that Zoom call with the banker. That wasn't just a small scheduling conflict that only affected me. That loan is what keeps the whole operation afloat for the entire year. My son comes back to help out during harvest, and he relies on the farm being financially stable. But I've put off several crucial farm decisions just like that one recently, entirely because I couldn't get myself looking... well, acceptable enough to sit down and negotiate with people. I just get so paralyzed by how awful and weathered my face and hands look that I end up putting our entire family's livelihood on hold. I mean, the guilt of that alone is heavy, but the fear of being stared at is somehow heavier.

And it’s the exact same thing with the side business I mentioned before, the retreat and the craft sales. My daughter actually helps my wife run the website for that. She's the one who set up that whole photography session I refused to do. She had this big vision, spent weeks organizing it, trying to get pictures of us to promote the homemade preserves—my wife makes this wonderful blackberry jam from her grandmother's recipe, and I used to do some wood carving that we'd sell in the gift shop—and my daughter kept saying they needed those photos of us working to really market the place properly. But I just completely shut it down. I stopped agreeing to any photos at all. 

I know it would help promote the sales and bring in that extra income for the family, which we really need when the crop yields are unpredictable, but I just... I can't let my daughter plaster my face and these ruined hands all over the internet for the whole world to scrutinize. I just can't do it. So, yes, it definitely causes tension with the kids, too. They don't understand why I'm being so stubborn and difficult about it, and I end up feeling like I'm letting the whole family down just because I can't bear to be seen.
Do you feel like your concerns about how you look are making it harder for you to enjoy time with your family or pursue activities you used to like?

Well, yes. It really does. It just... it takes the joy right out of everything, to be completely honest with you. I mean, even when the grandkids are over, which used to be the highlight of my week, you know? They’d come running up the dirt driveway, and I used to just scoop them up without a second thought. But now... well, kids are observant, aren't they? They don't have any sort of filter. A while back, my youngest grandson was sitting on my lap, and he just reached out and poked my hand and asked what all the dirt was that wouldn't wash off. He meant the sunspots, of course. And the deep cracks on my knuckles. And I know he's just a little boy, he didn't mean anything malicious by it, but... my stomach just completely dropped. I felt my face get hot. I couldn't even focus on playing with him or listening to his little stories after that. I just made an excuse about needing to check the barn and went into the other room. So even those precious moments, those family moments, they just get completely clouded over by this dread. 

And the things I used to do just for myself, for fun... like the wood carving I mentioned earlier. I used to absolutely love that. I'd sit out on the back porch in the evenings, especially in the late summer when the air finally starts to cool down, just me and a piece of good cedar and my carving knives. It was relaxing. It was my way to unwind and clear my head after being on the tractor all day. But now, if I try to sit down and carve, I can't even look at the wood. I'm just staring at my own hands holding the knife. I see every single deep line, the way the skin looks like old, ruined leather, the spots, the sagging... and I just lose all interest. The joy just evaporates. I end up putting the tools away. I haven't finished a single piece in I don't know how long. 

It's like this constant, loud buzzing in my head, doctor. It never stops. Even if we're just having a quiet Sunday dinner, my wife makes a roast, the kids are over... I'm sitting there at the head of the table, and instead of listening to my son talk about his week, I'm wondering if the overhead dining room light is casting shadows that make the sagging around my jaw look worse. I'm wondering if they're staring at my hands while I pass the potatoes. It just never turns off. You can't really enjoy anything—not a meal, not a hobby, not your own family—when your mind is entirely consumed by how awful you look. It just... it drains the life right out of you, it really does.
Is there one particular feature or flaw that bothers you the most, something that you think about more than any other when you're worried about how you look?

Well, I know I've been talking your ear off about it, and I know I touched on this right at the beginning, but if you're asking for the absolute worst of it... I really can't separate my face from my hands. It's both of them together. That's honestly the whole reason I finally made this appointment and came in today. I just... I absolutely cannot get past how unbelievably rough and worn my face and my hands look. It’s just constantly on my mind. 

If I had to narrow it down to the exact things, like I was saying before, it's the deep cracks on my knuckles, those awful dark spots, and that sagging skin around my neck and jaw. It’s just... it’s all of that combined. And the reason it bothers me more than anything else is because of how exposed it is. You can't hide your face and your hands, you know? When I'm sitting across a desk from a banker, or one of those county extension folks who come out to look at the property, I just know they're staring right at it. I'll be sitting there trying to talk about serious things, farm business, crop yields, and I can just feel their eyes locked onto the cracks and the spots and the sagging skin. It’s paralyzing. I feel like they aren't hearing a single word I say because they're too busy judging how damaged I look.

And I know I mentioned my wife earlier, but it just... it really frustrates me because she completely dismisses how bad it is. She just looks at me and says I look exactly like a man who’s worked outdoors his whole life. She thinks it's perfectly normal for a farmer to look like this, like it's just a badge of hard work or something. But she doesn't understand what it's like to be the one actually wearing this skin, feeling like everyone in town is just repulsed by it. So, to answer your question, it's not just one single tiny flaw, it's that whole rough, worn look on my face and hands... the spots, the cracks, the sagging. That's the thing that just completely consumes me.
Do you think other people actually notice or care about the flaws in your appearance as much as you think they do?

Well, yes, I absolutely do think they notice. I mean, like I was just trying to explain a minute ago, that's honestly what brings me in to see you today. I just... I cannot get past how rough and worn my face and hands look, and I am entirely convinced that other people are zeroing right in on it. 

You ask if they notice as much as I think they do, and I just don't see how they couldn't. When you're sitting across from someone, just a few feet away... I really do feel like every banker or county person I have to deal with is just sitting there staring right at the cracks, the spots, and the sagging skin. It's like their eyes are just drawn to it. I can see them glance down when I hand them a piece of paper, or I can see their eyes sort of dart around my jawline when I'm trying to explain a problem with the irrigation system. 

And, you know, this is exactly what I argue with my wife about all the time. I know I brought her up before, but she just completely brushes it off. She tells me I'm imagining it, that they aren't staring at all, even though my wife says I just look like a man who's worked outdoors his whole life. She says, "You're a farmer, you've been in the sun for forty years, you're supposed to have weathered skin." But she's not the one sitting in that chair. She doesn't feel the weight of it. She doesn't see the way these professionals look at me. 

It’s just so obvious to me that they care. It's not just a passing glance, it feels like this intense scrutiny, like they're judging my character or my competence based on how damaged my skin is. How are you supposed to negotiate a loan or talk about crop yields when you know the person across from you is just completely distracted by how awful you look? So, yes, I really do think they notice every single flaw. It's what drove me to finally make this appointment, because I just can't keep trying to do business when I know everyone is staring at me like that.
Do you think that if you were to cover up or hide the parts of your body that you're concerned about, people would still be staring at you or judging you?

Well, I try to hide it. I mean, you ask if covering it up helps, but the thing is, just trying to hide it becomes this whole... this whole exhausting ordeal. It doesn't really stop the feeling that people are judging me, because the process of trying to conceal it just takes over my life. 

Like, before I have to leave the property for a loan meeting at the bank, or, say, if I'm taking a table down at the county craft fair—back when I had enough finished pieces to actually set up a table, anyway—I just get completely stuck. I'll be in the house, standing in front of the bathroom mirror for I don't know how long, just staring at the sagging skin and the spots, trying to figure out how bad it looks in that light. And then I'll finally get out to the truck, but I can't even put the thing in drive. I'm checking the rearview mirror, then I'm leaning over to check the side mirror on the truck, and I'm just... I'm taking my cap and turning it this way and that way, pulling the brim down low, trying to see if I can get the shadow to fall just right so it hides the worst of my face. 

And my hands, well, you can't exactly wear heavy winter gloves into a bank in the middle of June without looking like a fool, so I just end up obsessing over them. I'll sit there in the cab of the truck, comparing my hands to the younger workers we have helping out on the property. I just picture their smooth skin and then look down at my own cracked, ruined knuckles and the dark spots, and it just makes me sick. I do this over and over—checking the mirror, adjusting the hat, looking at my hands, adjusting the hat again—until I look at the dashboard clock and realize I've wasted a good hour or more. It's time I should absolutely be using on the farm, getting actual work done, fixing the baler or checking the fence lines. 

And the most frustrating part of it all is that even after all that checking, and even if I manage to hide my face under the brim of my hat, the second I walk into that meeting or sit behind that craft-fair table, I still feel like they can see right through it. I still feel those eyes on me. So, hiding it... it doesn't really stop the judgment, it just completely derails my day before I've even left the driveway.
Do you ever think that your appearance is actually normal, and it's just your perception of it that's distorted?

Well, I try. I really, really do try to step back and ask myself that exact question. I'll be standing there in the bathroom, just looking in the mirror, and I'll actually try to force myself to see it the way you're suggesting. I'll try to hear my wife's voice in my head, because, like I've been telling you over and over today, she swears up and down that I just look like a normal man who's worked outdoors his whole life. She tells me it's completely natural for a farmer my age to have weathered skin, and I try to tell myself, "Okay, maybe she's right. Maybe it's just my own eyes playing tricks on me."

But the thing is... it never lasts. I just can't hold onto that thought for more than a few seconds. I look at myself, and I just can't see what she sees. And honestly, doctor, that is exactly what brings me in here to see you today. I am just so exhausted because I absolutely cannot get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. If it was just a little trick of the mind, I feel like I'd be able to talk myself out of it, you know? I'd be able to just say, "Well, the wife says I'm fine, so let's get on with the chores." 

But it doesn't feel distorted to me. It feels like cold, hard reality. When I leave the house, all that logic just completely evaporates. It doesn't feel like a distorted perception when I'm sitting in an office and I can feel that every banker or county person is just staring right at the cracks on my knuckles, the dark sun spots, and all that sagging skin around my jaw. I know I keep bringing up the bank and the county folks, but it's just because it dominates my entire life. I want to believe it's just in my head, I really do, but when I'm in those moments, the feeling that they are judging every inch of my damaged skin is just so overpowering that I can't convince myself it's normal.
Do you think that anyone has ever commented on your appearance in a way that suggests they find it as disturbing or abnormal as you do?

Well, no, not out loud. I mean, you ask if anyone has actually come right out and said something about how disturbing it is, and I have to admit, no, they haven't. But... well, you have to think about the kind of people I'm dealing with most of the time. I'm sitting across from a loan officer at the bank, or a county clerk, or even just the guys down at the feed store. People in professional settings, or even just folks around town, they aren't going to just look at a man and tell him his face looks ruined. That's just not how polite society works, right? They are trained to be professional, to keep a straight face, to smile and hand you the paperwork. 

But just because they don't say the words out loud doesn't mean I can't see the reaction. Like, I was at the hardware store a while back picking up some replacement parts for the tractor, just some basic hydraulic fittings, and the young kid behind the counter was ringing me up. He didn't say a single word about my hands. But when I reached out to hand him my card, I saw his eyes drop right down to my knuckles. I saw that little hesitation. He didn't tell me my skin looked like cracked leather, but the way he carefully took the card so our fingers wouldn't brush... well, that speaks volumes, doesn't it? 

My wife tells me I'm reading into it, that he was just looking at the credit card or the chip reader, but I know what I saw. So, no, nobody has explicitly commented on it. Nobody has pulled me aside and told me I look awful. But the silence almost makes it worse, honestly. It becomes this giant elephant in the room that everybody is too polite to mention, but we are all completely, acutely aware of it. And it just drives me crazy, because I'll be sitting there trying to talk about interest rates or soil samples, and my mind is just racing, just obsessing over the fact that I know they see it and I know they are judging it. So, no actual spoken comments, no. But the looks and the body language... that's more than enough.
Do you feel like your concerns about your appearance are significantly interfering with your ability to function in your daily life or enjoy activities you once found pleasurable?

Oh, Lord, yes. Yes, it absolutely is. I mean, I was just telling you about how it eats up my morning out in the truck, but it goes so much deeper than just wasting an hour here and there. It’s actually starting to hurt our livelihood, if I'm being completely honest with you. 

Take the farm, for instance. Running a property like ours, there are a million decisions to make every single week, and you can't just do it all in a vacuum. You have to talk to suppliers, you have to talk to the bank. But lately... well, I’ve been putting off major farm decisions because of all this. I've actually missed scheduled calls with our bankers. We had this big meeting set up not too long ago to discuss an equipment loan, and they like to do these video calls now, you know, ever since everything went online a couple years back. And I just... I couldn't do it. I spent the entire morning in the bathroom, and then in the office, trying to adjust the desk lamp, trying to find a shirt with a stiff collar that rides up high enough on my neck, just doing everything I could to make the sagging skin and the sun spots look less... horrifying. But I couldn't get myself looking acceptable enough to actually sit down and face those people on the screen. So I just didn't log on. I made up some excuse to my wife later about the internet being down, but the truth is, I just couldn't let them see me. 

And it’s not just the farm operations, it’s the extra stuff, too. My wife and I, we've been trying to get this little rural retreat going on the property to bring in some extra income, plus the craft sales I mentioned earlier—I do a bit of woodworking when I have the time. Well, to get people to come out all the way to our neck of the woods, you need marketing. You need a website, flyers, a Facebook page, that sort of thing. My wife keeps begging me to just let her take a few nice photos of us working the land, or me standing by the craft table with my finished pieces, just to show folks who we are. Give it that authentic, family-farm feel, she says. 

But I've completely stopped agreeing to photos. I flat out refuse. I can't stomach the thought of my ruined face and my cracked, leathery hands being plastered on a brochure or the internet for everyone to scrutinize. She tells me it would really help promote the retreat and the craft sales, and I know she's right, I really do. I know it's hurting the business when I won't participate. But the thought of that camera lens zooming in on all my flaws, freezing them in time for people to judge... I just can't do it. So, yes, doctor, it's... it's really paralyzing me. It's getting in the way of just about everything I used to do to keep this place running.
Do you think it's possible that your appearance is not as noticeable or disturbing to others as it is to you?

Well, I suppose... I mean, intellectually, maybe? I know I've been harping on this since I walked in the door, but like I was saying earlier, my wife tells me exactly that. She swears up and down that people aren't paying it any mind and that I just look like a normal man who's worked outdoors his whole life. She thinks it's just me blowing it all out of proportion. And I really, truly want to believe her. 

But... well, that is exactly what brings me in here today, doctor. I just absolutely cannot get past it. I can't get past how incredibly rough and worn my face and my hands look. It just doesn't feel like a possibility that they aren't noticing it, because to me, it's like a neon sign flashing right at them. When I have to go into town and I'm sitting across the desk from a banker, or some county zoning person, I can just feel it in my bones that they are staring right at every single crack on my knuckles, every dark sun spot on my cheeks, all that sagging skin hanging around my jawline. 

I try to tell myself, "Frank, maybe they're just looking at the paperwork, maybe they aren't scrutinizing you." But the feeling is just so heavy. It just dominates my thoughts. So, is it possible that it's less noticeable to them? Maybe in theory. But in my day-to-day life, out there in the real world, it feels completely impossible that they aren't seeing the exact same ruined skin that I see in the mirror every morning. I just can't shut off that feeling that everyone is zeroing in on the damage, no matter how much my wife tries to talk me down.
Is there a particular part of your body that you're most concerned about when it comes to your appearance?

Well, I know I've been sort of harping on them since I sat down, but it really boils down to two things mainly: my face and my hands. That’s really the whole crux of it. That’s exactly what brings me in here to see you, to be perfectly honest. I just... I absolutely cannot get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. It’s just this constant weight on my mind. 

I mean, you look at my hands, and I see these deep, awful cracks, the way the knuckles look so battered and leathery. And then my face... the sagging skin hanging around my jaw, the dark sun spots all over my cheeks from decades out on the tractor without a proper hat, back before we knew better about the sun. It's just ruined. 

And, you know, like I mentioned a minute ago, my wife, bless her heart, she tries her best to comfort me. She tells me, "Frank, you just look like a man who's worked outdoors his whole life. You look like a farmer, that's what hard work looks like." But I just can't accept that. I can't internalize it, because when I'm out in the world, when I'm sitting in those offices trying to get a zoning permit approved or talking to a banker or some county person, I don't feel like they're seeing a respectable, hardworking farmer. I feel like they are just sitting there staring right at the cracks on my fingers, or the spots and the sagging on my face. It’s like they can't look away from the damage. So, if you're asking what parts specifically are driving all this... it's definitely the face and the hands. That's what I just can't stop focusing on, day in and day out, no matter how much my wife tries to reassure me.
Do you think it's possible that your perception of your appearance is not based in reality?

Not based in reality... well, I mean, I hear what you’re asking, and I know I keep circling back to the exact same thing. I know I’m probably talking your ear off and sounding like a broken record here, but... the whole reason I'm sitting in this chair, what really brings me in to see you today, is that I simply cannot get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. 

You ask about reality, and, well, my wife, like I was just saying, she tells me my reality is completely skewed. She’ll sit me down at the kitchen table, pour me a cup of coffee, and say, "Frank, you just look like a man who's worked outdoors his whole life. You look like a farmer who's earned his keep." And she means it, she really does. I know she loves me. But then I step off the farm, and I have to sit across from a banker, or some county zoning person to talk about the property lines or the permits for that retreat we're trying to build, and my reality—the reality I am actually living and breathing in that exact moment—is that they are staring right at the deep cracks in my knuckles. They're staring at the sun spots, the sagging skin on my neck, all of it. I can literally feel their eyes just burning into the damage. 

So, is it possible my perception isn't reality? I mean, maybe intellectually, sure.
